  - "In the real browser test, infinite scroll grew from 20 to 100 items across 4 scrolls while pagination stayed at 20."

  - "Pagination gives every page its own crawlable, bookmarkable URL, while infinite scroll needs a paginated URL fallback for SEO."
  - "For very long lists, a virtualization library like TanStack Virtual combines an infinite feel with a flat DOM size."

<div id="bx-article">

  <div class="bx-pills">
    <span class="bx-pill">Development</span>
    <span class="bx-pill">JavaScript</span>
    <span class="bx-pill">Performance</span>
  </div>

  <p>Hello everyone! Today we're settling a debate that comes up on almost every list heavy page a project ever builds: infinite scroll vs pagination, and which one actually deserves the JavaScript implementation time. Real code and real browser numbers below, not just opinions.</p>

  <p class="bx-lede">Ever scrolled a feed so long you forgot how you even got there, then wished you could just jump back to page 3? That tension between two very different browsing experiences is exactly what this guide untangles, with working code for both.</p>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">01</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="infinite-scroll-vs-pagination-what-each-one-actually-does">Infinite Scroll vs Pagination: What Each One Actually Does</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>Pagination breaks a long list into fixed size pages, one page visible at a time, with next and previous controls moving between them. Infinite scroll vs pagination really comes down to one structural choice: does old content ever leave the page, or does everything just keep piling up underneath it.</p>

  <p>Infinite scroll instead appends each new batch of items onto the bottom of the same page as the visitor scrolls, never swapping anything out. Both approaches solve the same underlying problem, showing a large dataset without loading it all at once, in genuinely different ways.</p>

  <p>Neither option is universally correct, and the right pick tends to depend heavily on what the list actually contains. A social feed a visitor casually scrolls through leans toward infinite scroll, while a product catalog someone needs to compare, bookmark, or return to later leans hard toward pagination, a distinction worth pinning down before writing a single line of code.</p>

  <p>The infinite scroll vs pagination decision also shapes how much JavaScript actually ships to the browser. Pagination can work with almost no client side script at all, a server rendering each page fresh on request, while infinite scroll fundamentally depends on client side JavaScript to detect scroll position and fetch new data without a full page reload.</p>


  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">02</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="building-the-shared-batching-logic">Building the Shared Batching Logic</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>Both approaches can share the exact same underlying slicing logic. The only real difference is whether each new slice replaces the previous one or gets added on top of it.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">batching.js</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-kw">function</span> <span class="tok-fn">paginate</span>(<span class="tok-val">items</span>, <span class="tok-val">pageSize</span>, <span class="tok-val">pageNumber</span>) {
  <span class="tok-kw">const</span> <span class="tok-val">start</span> = (<span class="tok-val">pageNumber</span> - <span class="tok-val">1</span>) * <span class="tok-val">pageSize</span>;
  <span class="tok-kw">return</span> <span class="tok-val">items</span>.slice(<span class="tok-val">start</span>, <span class="tok-val">start</span> + <span class="tok-val">pageSize</span>);
}

<span class="tok-kw">function</span> <span class="tok-fn">accumulateForInfiniteScroll</span>(<span class="tok-val">items</span>, <span class="tok-val">pageSize</span>, <span class="tok-val">batchesLoadedSoFar</span>) {
  <span class="tok-kw">return</span> <span class="tok-val">items</span>.slice(<span class="tok-val">0</span>, <span class="tok-val">batchesLoadedSoFar</span> * <span class="tok-val">pageSize</span>);
}</code></pre>
  </div>

  <p><code>paginate</code> always returns a fixed size window, one page's worth of items. <code>accumulateForInfiniteScroll</code> returns a window that only ever grows, everything loaded up to that point. Run against 97 real items with a page size of 20, the difference in what ends up rendered is immediate.</p>

  <div class="bx-shot">
    <img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Real Node.js output comparing pagination, which always returns 20 items per page, against infinite scroll accumulation, which grows to 97 items after 5 batches">
  </div>
  <p class="bx-shot-caption">Actual output from the batching logic above, run against 97 real items.</p>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">03</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="implementing-infinite-scroll-with-intersectionobserver">Implementing Infinite Scroll With IntersectionObserver</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>A real infinite scroll implementation watches for a sentinel element near the bottom of the list and loads the next batch the moment it becomes visible, using the browser's built in <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/IntersectionObserver" target="_blank" rel="noopener"><code>IntersectionObserver</code></a>.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">infiniteScroll.js</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-kw">const</span> <span class="tok-val">observer</span> = <span class="tok-kw">new</span> IntersectionObserver(
  (<span class="tok-val">entries</span>) =&gt; {
    <span class="tok-kw">if</span> (<span class="tok-val">entries</span>[<span class="tok-val">0</span>].isIntersecting &amp;&amp; <span class="tok-val">loaded</span> &lt; <span class="tok-val">TOTAL</span>) {
      <span class="tok-fn">loadNextBatch</span>();
    }
  },
  { root: <span class="tok-val">scrollBox</span> }
);
<span class="tok-val">observer</span>.observe(<span class="tok-val">sentinelElement</span>);</code></pre>
  </div>

  <p>No scroll event listener or manual position math is needed here. The observer fires only when the sentinel actually enters view, which is both simpler to write and cheaper to run than checking scroll position on every single scroll event.</p>

  <div class="bx-tip">
    <span class="bx-tip-label">Tip</span>
    <p><code>IntersectionObserver</code> has been supported in every major browser for years, confirmed on <a href="https://caniuse.com/intersectionobserver" target="_blank" rel="noopener">caniuse.com</a>, so there is no fallback needed for a modern audience.</p>
  </div>

  <p>Chrome DevTools' <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/docs/devtools/performance/reference" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Performance Monitor panel</a> has a live "DOM Nodes" counter that climbs in real time as new batches load, a quick way to watch this exact effect happen live on any real page rather than only measuring it after the fact through a script.</p>

  <p>Driving a real browser through four real scrolls to the bottom of the list shows exactly what infinite scroll costs in DOM size, and lines that same measurement up against pagination navigating the identical dataset.</p>

  <div class="bx-shot">
    <img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Real Chromium output showing DOM item count growing from 20 to 100 across 4 real scrolls with infinite scroll, versus staying constant at 20 across 5 real page navigations with pagination">
  </div>
  <p class="bx-shot-caption">Real Chromium, real scrolling, real page navigation. One grows, one doesn't.</p>


  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">04</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="implementing-pagination-instead">Implementing Pagination Instead</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>A pagination implementation replaces the list content entirely on every navigation rather than appending to it, which is exactly why its DOM size never grows past one page's worth of items.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">pagination.js</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-kw">function</span> <span class="tok-fn">renderPage</span>(<span class="tok-val">pageNumber</span>) {
  <span class="tok-val">list</span>.innerHTML = <span class="tok-str">''</span>; <span class="tok-cm">// clear the previous page entirely</span>
  <span class="tok-kw">const</span> <span class="tok-val">pageItems</span> = <span class="tok-fn">paginate</span>(<span class="tok-val">items</span>, <span class="tok-val">PAGE_SIZE</span>, <span class="tok-val">pageNumber</span>);
  <span class="tok-val">pageItems</span>.forEach((<span class="tok-val">item</span>) =&gt; <span class="tok-val">list</span>.appendChild(<span class="tok-fn">buildRow</span>(<span class="tok-val">item</span>)));
}</code></pre>
  </div>

  <p>That single <code>list.innerHTML = ''</code> line is the entire mechanism behind pagination's flat memory profile. Nothing from an earlier page is ever kept around once a visitor moves on from it.</p>

  <p>Pagination also gets a real benefit infinite scroll has to work much harder for: a URL that can point directly at page 4, bookmarkable and shareable, typically implemented as a simple query parameter like <code>?page=4</code> that <code>renderPage</code> reads on load.</p>

  <p>Reading that same parameter back out on page load, then calling <code>renderPage</code> with it before anything else runs, is what makes a refreshed or directly shared pagination URL land a visitor on the exact page they expected instead of always resetting back to page one. That one extra step is easy to skip and just as easy to add.</p>

  <div class="bx-fact">
    <span class="bx-fact-label">Did You Know</span>
    <p>Google's own Search Central documentation on <a href="https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics" target="_blank" rel="noopener">JavaScript SEO basics</a> notes that content only reachable by scripted scroll events, with no crawlable link to it, risks never being indexed at all. A working infinite scroll needs a paginated URL fallback for exactly this reason.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">05</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="seo-and-accessibility-tradeoffs">SEO and Accessibility Tradeoffs</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>Pagination gives every page its own real URL for free, which a search crawler can follow, index, and rank independently. An infinite feed with no equivalent URLs leaves a crawler with nothing to follow past whatever loaded on the very first request.</p>

  <p>The fix most production infinite scroll implementations use is a hybrid: infinite scroll for the visible experience, paired with real paginated URLs underneath that a crawler, or a visitor who prefers them, can navigate directly, each one server rendering the same content that batch would have appended.</p>

  <p><a href="https://www.nngroup.com/articles/infinite-scrolling/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Nielsen Norman Group's research on infinite scroll</a> raises a second concern beyond crawling: a visitor who scrolls away and then hits the back button often loses their exact scroll position entirely, landing back at the top of a feed they had already scrolled through once.</p>


  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">06</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="performance-impact-dom-size-and-memory">Performance Impact: DOM Size and Memory</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>The real browser test above already proved the core tradeoff of infinite scroll vs pagination on performance: infinite scroll's DOM node count only ever goes up, pagination's never does. That gap matters more the longer a visitor stays on the page.</p>

  <div class="bx-table-wrap">
    <table class="bx-table">
      <thead>
        <tr style="background:#2b2b2b !important;">
          <th style="background:#2b2b2b !important; color:#ffffff !important;">Factor</th>
          <th style="background:#2b2b2b !important; color:#ffffff !important;">Infinite Scroll</th>
          <th style="background:#2b2b2b !important; color:#ffffff !important;">Pagination</th>
        </tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr><td>DOM node count over a long session</td><td>Keeps growing</td><td>Stays flat</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Crawlable URL per section</td><td>No, without extra work</td><td>Yes, built in</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Scroll position on back navigation</td><td>Often lost</td><td>Not applicable</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Implementation complexity</td><td>Higher, needs an observer</td><td>Lower, needs page routing</td></tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
  </div>

  <p>A page with thousands of accumulated DOM nodes also affects <a href="/what-is-total-blocking-time-tbt/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Total Blocking Time</a> and general responsiveness, since the browser has more elements to lay out, style, and keep track of on every single interaction, not just the initial load. <a href="https://web.dev/articles/dom-size" target="_blank" rel="noopener">web.dev's own guidance on DOM size</a> recommends staying under roughly 1,500 total nodes on a page, a ceiling raw infinite scroll can quietly blow past after enough scrolling.</p>

  <p>For a list that genuinely needs to feel infinite and also needs to scale past a few hundred items, a virtualization library like <a href="https://github.com/TanStack/virtual" target="_blank" rel="noopener">TanStack Virtual</a> renders only the rows currently visible in the viewport, unmounting the rest, combining the feel of infinite scroll with pagination's flat DOM footprint.</p>

  <p>That third option is worth knowing about even for a team that ultimately picks the plain infinite scroll vs pagination choice covered above, since it is the natural next step the moment either simple approach starts showing real performance problems in production rather than in a small test dataset.</p>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">07</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="common-mistakes-when-choosing-between-them">Common Mistakes When Choosing Between Them</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>Most infinite scroll vs pagination regrets trace back to one of these five decisions made without weighing the tradeoffs above.</p>

  <ul class="bx-checklist">
    <li><b>Shipping infinite scroll on a content heavy page with no crawlable URLs:</b> proven above to risk leaving most of that content unindexed entirely.</li>
    <li><b>Never unloading old batches on a very long feed:</b> DOM node count climbs without bound, proven above with a real 20 to 100 item growth across just 4 scrolls.</li>
    <li><b>Using infinite scroll where a visitor needs to compare or return to a specific item:</b> a shareable, bookmarkable page number serves that need far better than an endless feed does.</li>
    <li><b>Forgetting a loading indicator near the sentinel:</b> a visitor who scrolls faster than the next batch can load sees a dead stop with no feedback that more content is coming.</li>
    <li><b>Choosing infinite scroll purely because it feels modern:</b> a paginated product catalog, documentation index, or search results page usually serves visitors better than a feed ever would, a point <a href="https://css-tricks.com/pagination-and-infinite-scroll/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">CSS-Tricks covers well</a> alongside a walkthrough of both patterns.</li>
  </ul>

  <p>None of these mistakes require an infinite scroll vs pagination decision to be made all at once. A page can genuinely ship pagination first, since it is simpler to build correctly, and revisit infinite scroll later once the SEO and accessibility work needed to support it properly has a real place on the roadmap.</p>

    <div class="bx-faq">
    <h3 class="bx-h3">Frequently Asked Questions</h3>

    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">1</span><span>Infinite scroll vs pagination, which one is actually better for SEO?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Pagination, on its own merits, since every page gets a real crawlable URL. Infinite scroll needs a paginated URL fallback built in underneath it to match that, not the endless feed alone.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">2</span><span>Does infinite scroll always cause a memory problem?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Only if old batches are never removed from the DOM. A raw implementation like the one above does grow without bound, proven above, but a virtualization library keeps memory flat by unmounting offscreen rows.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">3</span><span>What triggers loading the next batch in infinite scroll?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>A sentinel element near the bottom of the list, watched by an IntersectionObserver, which fires the moment that element scrolls into view rather than requiring a manual scroll position check.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">4</span><span>Can both approaches share the same backend API?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Yes. Both examples above use the exact same slicing logic and the same page size and offset parameters, only the rendering behavior on the frontend differs between them.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">5</span><span>Is infinite scroll ever the clearly better choice?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Yes, for a genuinely endless, casually browsed feed where a visitor rarely needs to return to a specific earlier item, a social feed being the classic example.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">6</span><span>What is the simplest way to test which one performs better on a real page?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Measure DOM node count directly in the browser console with a query selector count, exactly like the real test above, rather than guessing from theory alone.</p></div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-learn">
    <h2 id="what-we-learn-today">What We Learn Today</h2>
    <div class="bx-learn-grid">
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">1</span><div><h4>Pagination replaces, infinite scroll appends</h4><p>One structural difference explains almost every other tradeoff.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">2</span><div><h4>DOM size only grows with infinite scroll</h4><p>Real proof: 20 to 100 items across 4 scrolls, pagination stayed at 20.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">3</span><div><h4>IntersectionObserver drives modern infinite scroll</h4><p>No manual scroll position math needed.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">4</span><div><h4>Pagination wins on crawlable URLs</h4><p>Infinite scroll needs an added fallback to match it.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">5</span><div><h4>Both can share one backend API</h4><p>Only the frontend rendering behavior actually differs.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">6</span><div><h4>Virtualization gets both benefits at once</h4><p>Infinite feel, flat DOM footprint, at the cost of a dependency.</p></div></div>
    </div>
  </div>


  <div class="bx-cta">
    <h3>Ready to Pick the Right One for Your Page?</h3>
    <p>Infinite scroll vs pagination doesn't need to be a guess. Real DOM node counts, real crawlability tradeoffs, and working code for both are above.</p>

</div>

<script>
(function() {
  var items = document.querySelectorAll('.bx-faq-item');

  items.forEach(function(item) {
    var q = item.querySelector('.bx-faq-q');
    var a = item.querySelector('.bx-faq-a');

    item.classList.add('open');
    a.style.maxHeight = a.scrollHeight + 'px';

    q.addEventListener('click', function() {
      var isOpen = item.classList.contains('open');
      if (isOpen) {
        item.classList.remove('open');
        a.style.maxHeight = null;
      } else {
        item.classList.add('open');
        a.style.maxHeight = a.scrollHeight + 'px';
      }
    });
  });
})();
</script>
